title: Console role management: define scope model (org vs project vs environment) and required UX behaviors
creator: Naomi Feldman
content:
Problem
We need a single, consistent scope model for RBAC v2 that (a) maps cleanly to product concepts (Hosted, Dedicated, Private), (b) can be expressed in the Console with minimal confusion, and (c) does not block the v1 Role Management MVP.

This ticket clarifies:
1) What scopes exist (org / project / environment / cluster) and which are in Console MVP.
2) How role assignments behave across scopes (inheritance rules, visibility, conflict handling).
3) How role templates are presented and applied.

Why now (context)
- Enterprise prospects (Dedicated + Private) are explicitly asking for separation of duties and scoped admin control (e.g., operator can manage deployments in one environment but not audit export org-wide).
- Engineering needs a stable target for endpoint annotations and policy evaluation caching (scope keys) and for role-template generation.
- Design needs final semantics for the scope picker, list views, and ‘why denied’ guidance.

Decision summary (final)
We will support a hierarchical scope model with explicit bindings at a specific scope, plus optional visibility of inherited access.

Canonical scopes (RBAC v2 primitives)
A Role Binding is always attached to exactly one scope.
- Org scope (org:ORG_ID)
  - Top-level administrative scope. Includes org-level settings and cross-project actions.
  - Examples: manage org users, create projects, configure org-wide audit log export destinations, manage SSO configuration.

- Project scope (org:ORG_ID, project:PROJECT_ID)
  - Applies to a single project and its environments.
  - Examples: manage API keys for a project, edit routing policies for that project, view project usage dashboards.

- Environment scope (org:ORG_ID, project:PROJECT_ID, env:ENV_ID)
  - Applies to a single environment within a project.
  - Used for production separation and safe delegation.
  - Examples: change rollout policy/model pinning for prod only, view prompts/evals tied to an environment.

- Cluster scope (private only; org:ORG_ID, deployment:DEPLOYMENT_ID, cluster:CLUSTER_ID)
  - Exists only for Private deployments where cluster-level operations are separated.
  - NOTE: Cluster scope will be supported in the RBAC model and API, but is not required for Console MVP (see below).

Inheritance and evaluation rules
- Effective permissions are the union of permissions granted by bindings at:
  - The exact scope of the request, plus
  - Its ancestors (Environment inherits from Project and Org; Project inherits from Org).
- There is no implicit downward creation of bindings (i.e., an org binding does not generate per-project bindings). We only compute effective access at evaluation time.
- There is no concept of “deny” roles in v2. Conflicts are resolved by union (allow-only model). Any future deny capability is out-of-scope.

Console MVP scope support (what we ship first)
In Console role management v1 we will support:
- Creating and managing custom roles at the org level (roles are org-owned).
- Creating role bindings for:
  - Org scope
  - Project scope
  - Environment scope
Not in Console MVP:
- Cluster-scope binding creation UI (Private). It can remain API-only initially.
- Any customer-exposed ABAC/policy language.

UX behavior requirements
1) Scope picker
- Role binding creation requires selecting a scope type (Org / Project / Environment) first.
- If Project is selected, user must choose a project.
- If Environment is selected, user must choose a project first, then an environment.
- For Private deployments, if the org has no projects/environments surfaced (e.g., cluster-only mode), Console should show “This deployment is administered via API/installer tooling” rather than presenting empty pickers.

2) Binding list views and “effective access” visibility
- Default list view shows bindings at the currently selected scope only (“Direct bindings”).
- Provide a toggle or secondary view to show “Inherited access” (computed):
  - Example: In an environment page, show org-level and project-level bindings that grant access to this environment.
- Rationale: admins need to answer “who can touch prod?” without accidentally editing a different-scope binding.

3) Guardrails to prevent accidental broad grants
- When user attempts to bind a powerful role (e.g., Org Admin / Security Admin) at Org scope, require an extra confirmation step.
- When user selects Org scope and chooses a role template that contains sensitive permissions (as flagged by sensitivity tier), show a callout that it applies across all projects/environments.
- We do not block the action (admins must be able to do it), but we make scope impact explicit.

4) Templates (built-in roles)
- Templates are defined once per org (shipped by policy bundle) and can be applied at any supported scope (Org/Project/Environment).
- The binding scope does not mutate the role; it only constrains where its permissions apply.
- Console template flow:
  - Step 1: select template
  - Step 2: select scope
  - Step 3: select subjects (users/groups/service accounts depending on deployment)
- If a template includes permissions that only make sense at Org scope (e.g., org-level SSO config), and the user selects Project/Environment scope:
  - Console should allow it but warn: “Some permissions in this role have no effect at this scope.”
  - This mirrors the underlying engine behavior and avoids “mystery failures.”

5) Subject types and group mapping (SSO)
- Console should treat “IdP group” as a first-class subject type for role bindings when SSO is enabled.
- For Console MVP, we will support:
  - User subjects (internal + external)
  - Group subjects (IdP groups)
- Service accounts can be added later; initial scope definition should not assume service accounts are present.

6) ‘Why was I denied?’ alignment
- Scope selection impacts denial messaging. If a user is denied at an environment-scoped action, Console should guide admins to:
  - Check environment bindings first
  - Then project
  - Then org
- This needs to align with denial reason codes and debug headers work (tracked separately) so the UI can point to the most likely missing binding scope.

Product semantics mapping (Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private)
Hosted + Dedicated
- “Project” maps to Redwood projects (customer-visible) where API keys, routing policies, and usage controls live.
- “Environment” maps to environments within a project (e.g., dev/staging/prod). If a customer has not enabled environments, we still keep the concept internally; Console can show a single default environment.

Private
- Private may be deployed in a single-cluster, single-env mode initially for some customers.
- Our RBAC model must support cluster scope for operators, but Console can defer this until we validate customer demand.
- Installer/bootstrap flows must ensure there is always at least one org-scoped admin binding (break-glass aside). Console must not assume it can create the first admin.

Open questions / follow-ups (non-blocking for this ticket)
- Do we need explicit “Environment Admin” vs “Deployment Operator” role templates to prevent customers from using Org Admin too broadly? (Likely yes; tracked in role template work.)
- How do we represent “default environment” in environments-disabled orgs? Proposed: a synthetic env called “default” with env_id=default. Needs engineering confirmation.
- Private cluster scope UI requirement: revisit after first two Private pilots.

Acceptance criteria
- [x] A written scope model is agreed with Security + Platform + Design, including inheritance.
- [x] Console MVP scope requirements are explicit (Org/Project/Environment supported; Cluster deferred).
- [x] Template behavior and warnings at narrower scopes are specified.
- [x] Clear requirements for binding list view vs effective access view are defined.
- [x] Links provided to design spec for implementation.

Notes / key discussion points
- Security (Marcus) strongly prefers environment scoping to prevent broad prod access by default. Agreement: environment scope is first-class in Console MVP.
- Platform (Jordan/Ethan) flagged caching and performance concerns if scope resolution is complex. Decision: fixed hierarchy, no custom graph; scope keys are deterministic.
- Design (Tessa) requested clear separation between “direct bindings” and “inherited access” to reduce accidental edits. Decision included above.

Updates / timeline
2025-01-24: Draft scope options shared in Slack; initial disagreement on whether environment is required for MVP.
2025-01-29: Workshop with Platform + Security: aligned on hierarchical model and union-only evaluation.
2025-02-04: Design review: added requirement for inherited access view and warnings for “no effect at this scope.”
2025-02-14: Final sign-off from Security + Platform sponsors; marked done and linked to Console UX spec for execution.

Sign-offs
- PM: Naomi Feldman
- Security Eng: Marcus Lin
- Platform Eng: Jordan Lee
- UX Lead: Tessa Morgan
comments: 2025-01-24 (Naomi Feldman): Posting first draft. Main question: do we need Environment scope in v1, or can we do Org+Project only and add Env later? I’m leaning Env in v1 because otherwise “who can touch prod” becomes messy.

2025-01-29 (Marcus Lin): +1 environment scope for least privilege; if we skip it, we’ll end up with broad project roles granting prod implicitly. Also aligns with enterprise separation-of-duties questionnaires.
2025-01-30 (Jordan Lee): From evaluator side, fixed hierarchy is fine. Please avoid arbitrary nesting or customer-defined graphs; we need deterministic scope keys for safe caching.
2025-02-04 (Tessa Morgan): For UI, we need two modes: show direct bindings vs show effective/inherited. Otherwise admins will edit org bindings while thinking they’re editing prod-only access.

2025-02-07 (Ethan Park): Confirming control plane endpoints can accept scope dimensions (org/project/env). We’ll need a consistent ID format for env; if environments aren’t enabled, we can use default env internally as Naomi suggested.
2025-02-14 (Naomi Feldman): Marking done. Captured warnings for templates applied at narrower scopes. Next step is to ensure DES-914 and implementation stories reference this definition.
